code:
!nvidia-smi
import torch

if torch.cuda.is_available():

why: Make sure Colab has allocated a GPU before you download anything. Your RTX 3050 at home is not being used by a cloud Colab runtime.
explanation: `!nvidia-smi` asks the NVIDIA driver about the GPU and its memory. The exclamation mark tells the notebook to execute a Linux shell command. `import torch` loads PyTorch, the library performing the GPU calculations. `torch.cuda.is_available()` tests whether it can access an NVIDIA GPU. The `if` block prints the hardware name and memory only if the check passes. `1024**3` converts bytes into gibibytes.

title: Install software inside Colab
why: Install the training libraries on the cloud computer. Installing them on Windows is not required.
explanation: `%pip` installs Python packages into the notebook environment. `unsloth` loads and fine tunes models using memory-saving methods. `datasets` handles training records. `trl` provides a supervised fine tuning trainer. `-q` asks for quieter output; `-U` asks for current compatible releases. Package versions may change; this is the most version-sensitive step.
expected: Installation finishes without a red error. You may see informational warnings about package versions.
check: If asked to restart, use Runtime > Restart session, then start running from Cell 01 again.
trouble: If dependencies conflict, use the installation cell from the latest official Unsloth Qwen3 Colab notebook. Do not mix old trainer examples with newer packages.

title: Import and set reproducible choices
code:
import random
import numpy as np
import torch
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel
from datasets import Dataset

SEED = 42
random.seed(SEED)
np.random.seed(SEED)
torch.manual_seed(SEED)
MAX_LENGTH = 512
MODEL_ID = "unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-unsloth-bnb-4bit"
print("Chosen checkpoint:", MODEL_ID)
why: Decide the model, random seed and the maximum length before training so you know exactly what was used.
explanation: `import` statements make functions available. `random`, NumPy and PyTorch have separate random-number sources. Setting them to 42 helps reproduce a run, although GPU software can still vary. `MAX_LENGTH=512` caps the text pieces used in one training record. `MODEL_ID` points to a real 4 bit Qwen3 0.6B model on Hugging Face. 0.6B means roughly 600 million parameters; it is an intentionally small practice model.
expected: You should see the printed checkpoint name.
check: In the lab report, write down model name, date, GPU type and version of the notebook.
trouble: If `unsloth` fails to import after installation, restart the Colab runtime and rerun the import cell.

title: Download the starting model
code:
model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name=MODEL_ID,
    max_seq_length=MAX_LENGTH,
    load_in_4bit=True,
    dtype=None,
)
print("Model and tokenizer loaded")
why: Load a pre-trained model before it learns anything from your examples. This is the baseline.
explanation: `FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained` downloads or reads the model. `model` holds the neural network; `tokenizer` turns words into numerical tokens and back again. `max_seq_length` controls the allowed training context. `load_in_4bit=True` stores base weights in an efficient format to save VRAM. This is NOT the same as training every parameter at 4 bit. `dtype=None` asks Unsloth to select a suitable calculation type for the GPU.
expected: Unsloth messages appear and finally Model and tokenizer loaded.
check: Leave `MODEL_ID` unchanged for the first experiment; changing it makes comparisons harder.
trouble: If download fails, check connectivity and the checkpoint URL. Some software versions or Colab GPUs require changes from the official notebook.

title: Create 48 training examples and 12 unseen tests
code:
train_topics = [
    ("variable", "a named place to store a value", "count = 3"),
    ("loop", "a way to repeat instructions", "for x in items: print(x)"),
    ("function", "a reusable block of code", "def add(a,b): return a+b"),
    ("list", "an ordered collection", "items = [1, 2]"),
    ("dictionary", "a set of named values", "person = {'age': 20}"),
    ("boolean", "a true or false value", "ready = True"),
    ("class", "a blueprint for objects", "class Car: pass"),
    ("exception", "a signal that something failed", "raise ValueError()"),
    ("API", "a way for software systems to communicate", "GET /products"),
    ("database", "an organized place to keep data", "SELECT * FROM users"),
    ("cache", "storage for results we may reuse", "cache['key'] = result"),
    ("queue", "a waiting line for work", "enqueue(job)"),
]
test_topics = [
    ("recursion", "a function calling itself", "factorial(n-1)"),
    ("index", "a structure that speeds up searching", "CREATE INDEX ix ON users(name)"),
    ("JSON", "a text format for structured information", '{"ok": true}'),
]
questions = ["Explain {}.", "What is {}?", "Define {} simply.", "Teach me {}."]

def build_rows(topics):
    records = []
    for term, meaning, example in topics:
        for q in questions:
            records.append({
                "question": q.format(term),
                "answer": f"Meaning: {meaning}.\nExample: {example}",
                "term": term,
            })
    return records

train_rows = build_rows(train_topics)
test_rows = build_rows(test_topics)
print("Training examples:", len(train_rows))
print("Unseen test questions:", len(test_rows))
print(train_rows[0])
why: Provide a small dataset without any external download or personal data. The training and test topics are deliberately different.
explanation: Each tuple is a topic, a short explanation and a code example. The loop creates four different questions per training topic. This yields 12 × 4 = 48 training records and 3 × 4 = 12 unseen test records. `train_rows` teaches the model the format; `test_rows` must NOT enter training. A test set containing merely reworded versions of training questions can exaggerate results, so even the *topics* are held out here. The sample is tiny on purpose and is not enough for a reliable production model.
expected: 48 training examples, 12 unseen questions, and one record printed as a Python dictionary.
check: Open several examples and check that every Meaning and Example is correct. Correct small data beats large incorrect data.
trouble: The JSON illustration uses double quotes, as valid JSON requires. Check the surrounding answer for correctness and simplicity.

title: Convert examples into the model’s chat format
code:
SYSTEM = (
    "You are a software tutor. Answer using exactly two lines: "
    "Meaning: ... and Example: ... . Keep the answer short."
)

def to_training_text(record):
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
        {"role": "user", "content": record["question"]},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": record["answer"]},
    ]
    text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False,
        enable_thinking=False,
    )
    return {"text": text}

train_dataset = Dataset.from_list(train_rows).map(to_training_text)
print(train_dataset[0]["text"][:800])
why: Teach the model who is speaking and which answer belongs to which question.
explanation: A chat model recognises speaker markers and special tokens. We create a *system* instruction (the general rule), a *user* question and the desired *assistant* answer. `tokenizer.apply_chat_template` inserts Qwen-compatible boundaries. `tokenize=False` means return readable text now; training tokenizes it later. `add_generation_prompt=False` means this is a completed example, not a request for the model to start speaking. `enable_thinking=False` requests Qwen3 non-thinking formatting for this simple task. `Dataset.from_list` turns Python dictionaries into dataset rows; `.map` transforms every row.
expected: You should see special message markers and the first training question plus the desired two-line answer.
check: Confirm that the final answer appears after the assistant marker and that no test question is included.
trouble: If `enable_thinking` is unsupported by your tokenizer version, follow the updated Qwen3 model/Unsloth chat-template guidance; use the same template for every comparison.

title: Ask the original model before training
code:
def generate_answer(question):
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
        {"role": "user", "content": question},
    ]
    inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True,
        enable_thinking=False, return_tensors="pt",
    ).to(model.device)
    model.eval()
    with torch.inference_mode():
        outputs = model.generate(
            input_ids=inputs,
            max_new_tokens=96,
            do_sample=False,
            pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
        )
    generated = outputs[0][inputs.shape[1]:]
    return tokenizer.decode(generated, skip_special_tokens=True).strip()

before = [generate_answer(row["question"]) for row in test_rows]
for q, answer in zip(test_rows[:3], before[:3]):
    print("QUESTION:", q["question"])
    print("BEFORE:", answer, "\n")
why: Record a baseline so you can test whether the training accomplished anything.
explanation: The function builds messages for an unseen question. `tokenize=True` converts text into the numbers the model sees; `.to(model.device)` moves numbers to the GPU. `model.eval()` switches off training-only behaviour. `torch.inference_mode()` disables gradient calculations to save memory. `generate` produces up to 96 new tokens; `do_sample=False` uses deterministic decoding. The slice `outputs[0][inputs.shape[1]:]` removes the prompt tokens so only the answer is returned. The list `before` stores all original answers.
expected: You see three printed baseline answers. Their quality may already be good, because the system instruction itself requests the two-line format.
check: Do not adjust the question text after this point. Use exactly the same 12 questions and generation settings after training.
trouble: If generation is slow, reduce `max_new_tokens`. If responses contain thinking markers, verify non-thinking chat formatting and parsing; do not compare mixed formats.

title: Attach a small trainable LoRA adapter
code:
model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(
    model,
    r=8,
    lora_alpha=16,
    lora_dropout=0,
    bias="none",
    target_modules=[
        "q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",
        "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj",
    ],
    use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth",
    random_state=SEED,
)
print("LoRA adapter attached")
why: Train only a small set of extra weights instead of retraining every number in the model.
explanation: `get_peft_model` adds the small trainable LoRA components. `r=8` determines their size; a larger rank generally trains more values. `lora_alpha=16` controls their scaling. `lora_dropout=0` is a common Unsloth starting setting. `target_modules` says which internal layers receive adapters; leave these values alone as a beginner. `use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth"` trades extra computation for less memory usage. `random_state` makes adapter initialisation more repeatable. The original compressed model is mostly frozen.
expected: A message confirms an adapter was added; some versions print trainable parameter counts.
check: We are fine tuning with LoRA and a 4 bit base, often called QLoRA, not teaching a 27B model from scratch.
trouble: If a target-module error appears, copy the Qwen3 configuration from Unsloth’s maintained example notebook.

title: Configure the trainer
code:
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig

settings = SFTConfig(
    output_dir="qwen_lab_checkpoints",
    dataset_text_field="text",
    max_length=MAX_LENGTH,
    packing=False,
    per_device_train_batch_size=1,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    max_steps=30,
    learning_rate=2e-4,
    logging_steps=5,
    save_steps=30,
    fp16=not torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(),
    bf16=torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(),
    report_to="none",
    seed=SEED,
)
trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    processing_class=tokenizer,
    train_dataset=train_dataset,
    args=settings,
)
print("Trainer configured")
why: Tell the trainer what to read, how many updates to make, and how cautiously to learn.
explanation: `SFTTrainer` is the supervised fine tuning manager. `SFTConfig` stores the settings. `output_dir` is where intermediate results go. `dataset_text_field="text"` chooses the column built in Cell 06. `max_length` bounds sequence length. `packing=False` makes samples easier to reason about. `per_device_train_batch_size=1` processes one example at a time on the GPU, saving memory; `gradient_accumulation_steps=4` combines four such passes before one update. `max_steps=30` limits this educational run to 30 optimisation steps. `learning_rate=2e-4` controls weight-adjustment size. `logging_steps=5` prints loss regularly. `save_steps=30` saves a checkpoint near the end. `fp16`/`bf16` chooses precision supported by the GPU. `report_to="none"` stops optional experiment trackers. `processing_class=tokenizer` is the modern TRL argument.
expected: Trainer configured, possibly after Unsloth or TRL status messages.
check: Write down the settings before any tuning. If you adjust three settings simultaneously you will not know what caused an outcome.
trouble: TRL changes argument names over time. If you see “unexpected keyword”, use one supported version set from Unsloth’s maintained notebook, not a mix of old and new snippets.

title: Run the actual fine tuning
why: This is the step that actually changes the new trainable weights using your examples.
explanation: `trainer.train()` feeds token sequences through the model, predicts what text comes next, compares predictions with the desired training text, calculates an error called **loss**, and updates the LoRA weights to reduce that error. Thirty steps with four accumulated mini batches means approximately 120 example presentations, with repeated exposure to the 48 training records. `training_result.metrics` prints the summary. Training on tiny repetitive data can overfit very quickly.
expected: Progress and loss messages appear; the run ends with a dictionary containing training metrics. No specific final loss value is guaranteed.
check: A decreasing training loss indicates the model is getting better at predicting *training text*, but it does not prove it answers new questions correctly.
trouble: If CUDA runs out of memory, restart and reduce MAX_LENGTH to 256, rank to 4 or reduce other memory demands. If interrupted, you may need to rerun from loading the model.

title: Repeat the same unseen questions
code:
after = [generate_answer(row["question"]) for row in test_rows]
for row, old, new in zip(test_rows[:4], before[:4], after[:4]):
    print("QUESTION:", row["question"])
    print("BEFORE:", old)
    print("AFTER:", new, "\n")
why: Observe behavioural changes on questions and topics the trainer never saw.
explanation: This deliberately reuses the existing `generate_answer` function and the unchanged `test_rows`. `before` was computed from the original model; `after` is computed once the LoRA weights have been updated. Keeping the prompt, tokenizer, generation settings and test questions constant makes the comparison fairer.
expected: Four before-and-after pairs print. They may or may not improve: a small experiment has no guaranteed success.
check: Look for hallucinated code, missing Meaning/Example labels, unnecessary extra lines and incorrect definitions.
trouble: If answers are unchanged, that is still a useful result: try a better, more varied dataset, or compare without the strict system-format instruction.

title: Score the outputs and save an evaluation CSV
code:
import csv

def format_ok(answer):
    lines = [line.strip() for line in answer.splitlines() if line.strip()]
    return (len(lines) == 2 and
            lines[0].startswith("Meaning:") and
            lines[1].startswith("Example:"))

before_score = sum(format_ok(x) for x in before) / len(before)
after_score = sum(format_ok(x) for x in after) / len(after)
print(f"Before format score: {before_score:.1%}")
print(f"After  format score: {after_score:.1%}")

with open("qwen_lab_evaluation.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["question", "before", "after", "before_format_ok", "after_format_ok"])
    for row, old, new in zip(test_rows, before, after):
        writer.writerow([row["question"], old, new, format_ok(old), format_ok(new)])
print("Saved qwen_lab_evaluation.csv")
why: Turn a subjective impression into a simple, auditable result. Keep your raw responses for later inspection.
explanation: `format_ok` checks whether there are exactly two nonempty lines, with the requested labels. The percentages are computed over all 12 test questions. `csv.writer` saves each question and both responses to a local report file. **Important:** this metric tests formatting only; it does not measure whether the explanations or code snippets are correct. Because the system prompt already specifies the format, the baseline score may be 100%. A score of 100% after training therefore does not prove that fine tuning helped.
expected: Two scores print between 0% and 100%, and a CSV file appears in the Colab file sidebar.
check: For a proper review, manually grade meaning accuracy and example correctness (0 or 1 each), and try 20+ genuinely new questions.
trouble: If scores are equal, test without the exact-format system instruction and compare again; otherwise prompting and fine tuning can be confused.

title: Save and download the LoRA adapter
code:
model.save_pretrained("qwen_tutor_adapter")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("qwen_tutor_adapter")
!zip -qr qwen_tutor_adapter.zip qwen_tutor_adapter
from google.colab import files
files.download("qwen_tutor_adapter.zip")
why: Do not lose the weights when the temporary Colab session shuts down.
explanation: `save_pretrained` writes the trained LoRA adapter and tokenizer configuration to a folder. The `zip` shell command compresses the folder. `files.download` asks your browser to save that ZIP to your own computer. The ZIP contains the adapter, **not necessarily a standalone full model**; using it later requires the compatible original Qwen checkpoint. Colab files can disappear when a runtime resets.
expected: A browser download prompt appears. Save the ZIP somewhere safe, not only in Colab.
check: Unzip and confirm there is an adapter config and at least one adapter weights file.
trouble: If the download popup is blocked, use the Colab Files sidebar or copy the ZIP to mounted Google Drive.

title: Optional: export the full result to GGUF
code:
# Run ONLY if you want to use the tuned model in Ollama.
# Export can take extra RAM, VRAM, disk space and time.
model.save_pretrained_gguf(
    "qwen_tutor_gguf", tokenizer,
    quantization_method="q4_k_m",
)
import glob
print(glob.glob("qwen_tutor_gguf/*.gguf"))
why: Create a file format that Ollama can load as a complete inference model.
explanation: `save_pretrained_gguf` asks Unsloth to combine/export the learned result and convert it to GGUF, a common local inference format. `q4_k_m` is a practical 4 bit output compression method; it is independent of the LoRA rank. `glob` lists the actual generated filenames. This export is **optional** because a free Colab runtime may not have enough memory or disk space for conversion, even when training succeeded.
expected: If successful, the printed list contains a .gguf filename inside qwen_tutor_gguf.
check: Keep the exact printed filename for the Ollama Modelfile. Do not guess it.
trouble: If GGUF conversion runs out of memory, stop: the training experiment is still complete. Keep the adapter ZIP and follow Unsloth’s current export guide another day.
